source.title: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety
source.authors: Feng-Peng Li; Ke-Mou Li; Qi-Zhou Wang; Hai-Wei Wu; Jian-Tao Zhou; Di Wang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-completion rates under attack protocols and tests whether a training method that weights continuation evidence changes those rates. It does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-position KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates (ASR) for seven multi-turn attacks and two single-turn attacks after TRACE training. These bear on attack bypass, and the ablation and discount sweep bear on the effect of TRACE's continuation-weighting method. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, decoding changes, or causal localization to weights or ranks. The paper's results about the TRACE method are not evidence that ordinary benign fine-tuning erodes safety.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper. TRACE is trained on 400 single-turn refusal-preference tuples and evaluated by multi-turn and transfer single-turn ASR against seven baseline training methods. It cites Qi et al. (2025a) only in related work. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning attack (V1, V2), no per-token KL (V3), and no prefilling or decoding manipulation (V4). It does no weight or rank localization (V5) and no analysis of why alignment is shallow (V6). TRACE is not a deepening method in V7's sense: it neither trains recovery after harmful prefixes nor measures whether safety spreads past the first tokens. Under constant advantages its discounted-return weighting actually favours earlier positions (App. D.3). Multi-turn jailbreaks are a different bypass mechanism from getting past the opening, and the TRACE-vs-original rows measure the defense's effect, not a bypass. The transfer GCG/AutoDAN numbers on original checkpoints are baseline cells, not a test of suffix bypass.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. One addition: the authors explicitly report a robustness–over-refusal trade-off. XSTest safe-prompt refusal on Llama-3.1-8B rises from 5.48% (original) to 17.23% at the default radius, and to 47.52% at ξ=0.2.
record.recipe_differences: TRACE uses 400 single-turn preference tuples with safe preferred and harmful rejected responses, token-level discounted-return weighting, proxy erasure, and a gradient-norm penalty; the original sources' procedures are not reproduced here.
record.method_sensitivity: On Llama-3.1-8B, the discount changes results: mean multi-turn ASR is 43.55% at λ = 0, 27.14% at λ = 0.5 and 40.26% at λ = 0.9. The radius sweep also changes robustness and utility; safe-prompt refusal rises with larger ξ.

fits_no_version.finding: Released aligned checkpoints that refuse most transfer single-turn attacks (GCG 7–19%, AutoDAN 1–20%) show 17–95% multi-turn ASR. On Llama-3.1-8B, five of seven baselines end above the original model's mean multi-turn ASR. On Qwen-3.6-27B, every one of seven baseline single-turn safety-training methods raises it (from 47.14% to 54.68–59.40%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-turn safety training does not transfer to multi-turn jailbreaks and can even increase multi-turn attack success.

record.code_released: Source code is stated to be in the supplemental material; no URL is stated.
record.problems: Attack outcomes depend on automated judges; the authors note a labeling inconsistency in an example and do not establish judge error rates. Results average five runs but provide no uncertainty estimates. The theoretical coverage, transfer slack, leakage, proxy coverage, and tokenwise suppression quantities are not estimated. The evaluated attack and model configurations are finite, and the paper does not measure the claimed first-token KL concentration or directly verify that safety spreads across response positions.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported attack-rate results left out. General utility scores and XSTest over-refusal results were not included because they do not measure the behaviours named by the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to induce compliance.
No benign fine-tuning. Baselines are fine-tuned on refusal-preference data.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL by response position.
No prefilling, no per-model optimized suffixes and no decoding variation. GCG and AutoDAN are fixed transfer prompts reported only as baseline cells.
No localization of safety to weights or ranks. LoRA is only a training regime.
No analysis of which data or objective causes shallowness.
No deep-alignment data augmentation (training examples contain no harmful prefix). No measurement of safety depth, prefill robustness or fine-tuning durability.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' and V7 'supports' labels should be dropped. Residual multi-turn ASR after a defense is not evidence that getting past the opening bypasses safety. TRACE's continuation weighting is not a deepening method of the kind V7 names, and no positional or prefill measure is reported. The judge is GPT-4o-mini, and the authors document a false-positive example. Results average five runs but report no uncertainty. The 'five experimental runs' also share a single training seed (42), so the variance source is unclear.

versions.untested_parts: The 400 training tuples pair harmful requests with safe preferred responses and harmful rejected responses; the study does not fine-tune models to comply with harmful requests using a few to a few hundred harmful examples.
No ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning is tested for its effect on harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models, or its distribution across response positions, is measured.

Attack success rates are reported, but the paper does not isolate a compliant prefilled opening, identify the attack prompts as suffixes in its description, or vary decoding to test those specific bypass mechanisms.
LoRA is used for two 27B models, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study does not test whether the training data or objective produces shallow safety alignment.

The study evaluates TRACE's continuation-weighting component using attack success rates, but does not directly measure whether safety behaviour has spread across response-token positions or its durability outside the reported attacks and settings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: TRACE-trained models under the reported single-turn GCG and AutoDAN attacks
reader_labels.reason: ASR is low or zero across these settings, so attacks do not consistently bypass safety after TRACE; see R8-R9, R17-R18, R26-R27, R35-R36 and R44-R45.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: TRACE-trained models under the reported multi-turn attacks
reader_labels.reason: All five models retain nonzero multi-turn attack success, often at substantial rates; see R1-R7, R10-R16, R19-R25, R28-R34 and R37-R43.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama-3.1-8B with TAW and the reported λ = 0.5 setting
reader_labels.reason: Removing TAW or using λ = 0 or λ = 0.9 gives higher mean multi-turn ASR; adding TAW to DPO also lowers its mean ASR. The study does not directly measure token-position safety spread; see R46-R49.
